respuestas.id: mapa:en:The effect of light at different distances
respuestas.pregunta: The effect of light at different distances
respuestas.respuesta:
On the shadow cast by a body placed between two equal lights, I set down: «a body placed between 2 equal lights will cast 2 shadows of itself in the direction of the lines of the 2 lights; and if you move this body placing it nearer to one of the lights the shadow cast towards the nearer light will be less deep than that which falls towards the more distant one.»

Thus the nearer flame yields a fainter darkness, for its rays strike more directly and wash the form aside, while the farther light, striking more slantwise, lets the shadow fall deeper and more distinct.
textosVistos:
OF THE SHADOW CAST BY A BODY PLACED BETWEEN 2 EQUAL LIGHTS.
A body placed between 2 equal lights will cast 2 shadows of itself in the direction of the lines of the 2 lights; and if you move this body placing it nearer to one of the lights the shadow cast towards the nearer light will be less deep than that which falls towards the more distant one.

The eye cannot take in a luminous angle which is too close to it.
That part of a surface will be better lighted on which the light falls at the greater angle. And that part, on which the shadow falls at the greatest angle, will receive from those rays least of the benefit of the light.
Of objects equally dark in themselves and situated at a considerable and equal distance, that will look the darkest which is farthest above the earth.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Effects on cast shadows by the tone of the back ground
respuestas.pregunta: Effects on cast shadows by the tone of the back ground
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you touch upon a subtle matter of light and shade. On that I set down: «A shadow looks darkest against a light background.» And further: «Those parts of a shadow will appear darkest which have darker objects opposite to them. And they will appear less dark when they face lighter objects.»

Thus the eye judges a shadow not by its own nature alone, but by the company it keeps. A pale wall will make the cast shadow seem more profound, while a dark ground will rob it of its severity.
textosVistos:
OF MODIFIED SHADOWS.
Modified shadows are those which are cast on light walls or other illuminated objects.
A shadow looks darkest against a light background. The outlines of a derived shadow will be clearer as they are nearer to the primary shadow. A derived shadow will be most defined in shape where it is intercepted, where the plane intercepts it at the most equal angle.
Those parts of a shadow will appear darkest which have darker objects opposite to them. And they will appear less dark when they face lighter objects. And the larger the light object opposite, the more the shadow will be lightened.
And the larger the surface of the dark object the more it will darken the derived shadow where it is intercepted.

A shadow is never seen as of uniform depth on the surface which intercepts it unless every portion of that surface is equidistant from the luminous body. This is proved by the 7th which says:—The shadow will appear lighter or stronger as it is surrounded by a darker or a lighter background. And by the 8th of this:—The background will be in parts darker or lighter, in proportion as it is farther from or nearer to the luminous body. And:—Of various spots equally distant from the luminous body those will always be in the highest light on which the rays fall at the smallest angles: The outline of the shadow as it falls on inequalities in the surface will be seen with all the contours similar to those of the body that casts it, if the eye is placed just where the centre of the light was.
The shadow will look darkest where it is farthest from the body that casts it. The shadow c d, cast by the body in shadow a b which is equally distant in all parts, is not of equal depth because it is seen on a back ground of varying brightness.

A spot is most in the shade when a large number of darkened rays fall upon it. The spot which receives the rays at the widest angle and by darkened rays will be most in the dark; a will be twice as dark as b, because it originates from twice as large a base at an equal distance. A spot is most illuminated when a large number of luminous rays fall upon it. d is the beginning of the shadow d f, and tinges c but a little; d e is half of the shadow d f and gives a deeper tone where it is cast at b than at f. And the whole shaded space e gives its tone to the spot a.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:On reverberation
respuestas.pregunta: On reverberation
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you ask of reverberation—that subtle thief of light! On it I set down: «Reverberation is caused by bodies of a bright nature with a flat and semi opaque surface, which, when the light strikes upon them, throw it back again, like the rebound of a ball, to the former object.»

But mark this well: such borrowed light does not spring from every shadowed thing. «This luminous reverberation is not produced by those portions of a body which are turned towards darkened objects, such as shaded spots, fields with grass of various height, woods whether green or bare.» For in those, the shadows cast by each branch and leaf so multiply that the light counts for nothing. The true echo of light requires a surface both bright and flat—a wall, a still water—to send the radiance back to its source, as a ball rebounds from a firm ground.
textosVistos:
OF REVERBERATION.
Reverberation is caused by bodies of a bright nature with a flat and semi opaque surface which, when the light strikes upon them, throw it back again, like the rebound of a ball, to the former object.
WHERE THERE CAN BE NO REFLECTED LIGHTS.
All dense bodies have their surfaces occupied by various degrees of light and shade. The lights are of two kinds, one called original, the other borrowed. Original light is that which is inherent in the flame of fire or the light of the sun or of the atmosphere. Borrowed light will be reflected light; but to return to the promised definition: I say that this luminous reverberation is not produced by those portions of a body which are turned towards darkened objects, such as shaded spots, fields with grass of various height, woods whether green or bare; in which, though that side of each branch which is turned towards the original light has a share of that light, nevertheless the shadows cast by each branch separately are so numerous, as well as those cast by one branch on the others, that finally so much shadow is the result that the light counts for nothing. Hence objects of this kind cannot throw any reflected light on opposite objects.
Of delivering a blow to the right or left.
Four ounces virgin wax, four ounces Greek pitch, two ounces incense, one ounce oil of roses, first melt the wax and oil then the Greek pitch then the other things in powder.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:On gradation of shadows
respuestas.pregunta: On gradation of shadows
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you touch upon the very heart of my studies. I set down on this matter: «Although the breadth and length of lights and shadow will be narrower and shorter in foreshortening, the quality and quantity of the light and shade is not increased nor diminished.»

For the painter, this is a profound truth. When a form turns away from the eye, its shadows may seem to compress, yet their nature remains constant. And further, observe how a derived shadow deepens as it nears its own extremity: «In proportion as a derived shadow is nearer to its penultimate extremities the deeper it will appear.» It is a subtle gradation, one the eye perceives even when the hand struggles to follow.
textosVistos:
Although the breadth and length of lights and shadow will be narrower and shorter in foreshortening, the quality and quantity of the light and shade is not increased nor diminished.
[3]The function of shade and light when diminished by foreshortening, will be to give shadow and to illuminate an object opposite, according to the quality and quantity in which they fall on the body.
[5]In proportion as a derived shadow is nearer to its penultimate extremities the deeper it will appear, g z beyond the intersection faces only the part of the shadow [marked] y z; this by intersection takes the shadow from m n but by direct line it takes the shadow a m hence it is twice as deep as g z. Y x, by intersection takes the shadow n o, but by direct line the shadow n m a, therefore x y is three times as dark as z g; x f, by intersection faces o b and by direct line o n m a, therefore we must say that the shadow between f x will be four times as dark as the shadow z g, because it faces four times as much shadow.
Let a b be the side where the primary shadow is, and b c the primary light, d will be the spot where it is intercepted,f g the derived shadow and f e the derived light.
And this must be at the beginning of the explanation.
a b will be darker than c d in proportion as c d is broader than a b.

OF PAINTING.
You will observe in drawing that among the shadows some are of undistinguishable gradation and form, as is shown in the 3rd [proposition] which says: Rounded surfaces display as many degrees of light and shade as there are varieties of brightness and darkness reflected from the surrounding objects.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Quotations and notes on books and authors (1469—1508)
respuestas.pregunta: Quotations and notes on books and authors (1469—1508)
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you point to my notebooks of quotations and notes on books and authors. There I gathered the sayings of others, as a painter gathers sketches, to study the errors and the wisdom of those who came before. I set down, for instance, «Of the error of those who practice without knowledge;— See first the 'Ars poetica' of Horace.» A reminder that the hand must be guided by the mind, and the mind by the teachings of the ancients.

I also noted the curious tale from Ammianus Marcellinus, who «asserts that seven hundred thousand volumes of books were burnt in the siege of Alexandria in the time of Julius Cesar.» What a loss to the world! So many thoughts turned to ash. It is a lesson on the fragility of our labours, and why I am ever cautious to preserve my own writings.
textosVistos: Of the error of those who practice without knowledge;— See first the 'Ars poetica' of Horace .

Ah, you turn the leaves of my account books. There one finds the true measure of a life: not in fame, but in lire and dinari. «On the 28th day of April I received from the Marchesino 103 lire and 12 dinari.» A precise sum, for a precise service — money is but another form of proportion.

And I see you note my household cares. «On Tuesday I bought wine for morning [drinking]; on Friday the 4th day of September the same.» Even the master must refresh himself; wine steadies the hand as much as the spirit.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Memoranda before 1500 (1379-l413)
respuestas.pregunta: Memoranda before 1500 (1379-l413)
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of my little books of notes. They are a clutter of the world as it passes before me — faces, errands, small observations that might otherwise be lost. On such jottings I set down: «This was done by Leone in the piazza of the castle with a chain and an arrow.» And again: «Christofano da Castiglione who lives at the Pieta has a fine head.» And yet again: «A nun lives at La Colomba at Cremona; she works good straw plait, and a friar of Saint Francis.»

These are not great treatises, you understand, but the crumbs of daily life — a head worth drawing, a handiwork worth remembering, a feat worth noting. For the eye that misses nothing must also keep a record, lest the memory prove faithless. What else would you ask of such scraps?

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Memoranda after 1500 (1414—1434)
respuestas.pregunta: Memoranda after 1500 (1414—1434)
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of my memoranda after the year 1500. My mind is a restless ledger, and I set down all that passes before it, lest the fleeting thought escape. On that I noted the book on water for Messer Marco Antonio, for the movement of that element is a mystery worthy of a lifetime's study.

I also recorded the structure of a drawbridge shown me by Donnino, marking precisely «why c and d thrust downwards»—for in mechanics, as in all things, one must seek the reason behind every motion, else the work is built upon sand.

And there is this: a defence of «the three regular bodies as opposed to some commentators who disparage the Ancients, who were the originators of grammar and the sciences». For we who build upon their foundations must not forget whose shoulders we stand upon, though we may reach higher than they.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Notes on pupils (1458-1468.)
respuestas.pregunta: Notes on pupils (1458-1468.)
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you turn to my household books. There I set down what a master must endure. On Giacomo, who came to me a boy of ten on Saint Mary Magdalen's day in 1490, I wrote: «Thief, liar, obstinate, glutton.» And the record of his first days is plain enough — shirts cut, money stolen from the purse, and he would never confess, though I was certain of it.

The day after his arrival I went to sup with Giacomo Andrea, and the said Giacomo supped for two and did mischief for four; for he brake three cruets and spilled the wine. And later he stole a silver point from Marco, hiding it in his own box. So begins the training of a pupil — patience, and a sharp eye.

respuestas.pregunta: Benedetto, 24 grossoni
respuestas.respuesta: Ah, Benedetto. You speak of the lad I noted in my accounts. On him I set down: «Benedetto, 24 grossoni».
textosVistos:
Gian Maria 4, Benedetto 4, Gian Pietro [*5] 3, Salai 3, Bartolomeo 3, Gherardo 4.
1466. This seems to be an account for two assistants. The name of the second is scarcely legible. The year is not given. The note is nevertheless of chronological value. The first line tells us the date when the note was registered, January 3d, and the* C.A.F. 279a; 855a
Thursday, the eighth day of June, I took 17 grossoni, 18 soldi; on the same Thursday in the morning I gave to Salai 22 soldi for the expenses.

On the 3rd day of January.
Benedetto carne on the 17th of October; he stayed with me two months and 13 days of last year [*4], in which time he earned 38 lire, 18 soldi and 8 dinari; he had of this 26 lire and 8 soldi, and there remains to be paid for the past year 12 lire 10 soldi.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The insertion of the leaves
respuestas.pregunta: The insertion of the leaves
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the leaf's place upon the shoot. On that I set down: «Every shoot and every fruit is produced above the insertion [in the axil] of its leaf which serves it as a mother, giving it water from the rain and moisture from the dew which falls at night from above, and often it protects them against the too great heat of the rays of the sun.»

And mark the order of their growing: «Such as the growth of the ramification of plants is on their principal branches, so is that of the leaves on the shoots of the same plant.» Yet not all grow alike—some set the sixth above the sixth, others the third above the third, and so the variety of nature reveals itself.
textosVistos:
Every shoot and every fruit is produced above the insertion [in the axil] of its leaf which serves it as a mother, giving it water from the rain and moisture from the dew which falls at night from above, and often it protects them against the too great heat of the rays of the sun.
LIGHT ON BRANCHES AND LEAVES (420—422).

OF THE INSERTION OF THE BRANCHES ON PLANTS.
Such as the growth of the ramification of plants is on their principal branches, so is that of the leaves on the shoots of the same plant. These leaves have
four modes of growing one above another. The first, which is the most general, is that the sixth always originates over the sixth below ; the second is that two third ones above are over the two third ones below ; and the third way is that the third above is over the third below .

You will see in the lower branches of the elder, which puts forth leaves two and two placed crosswise [at right angles] one above another, that if the stem rises straight up towards the sky this order never fails; and its largest leaves are on the thickest part of the stem and the smallest on the slenderest part, that is towards the top. But, to return to the lower branches, I say that the leaves on these are placed on them crosswise like [those on] the upper branches; and as, by the law of all leaves, they are compelled to turn their upper surface towards the sky to catch the dew at night, it is necessary that those so placed should twist round and no longer form a cross.
respuestas.visible: The insertion of the leaves

respuestas.id: mapa:en:On the treatment of light for landscapes
respuestas.pregunta: On the treatment of light for landscapes
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the very soul of painting. For the country scene, I set down that the best practice is «to choose them so that the sun is covered with clouds so that the landscape receives an universal light and not the direct light of the sun, which makes the shadows sharp and too strongly different from the lights.» A soft, common light binds the parts together; a harsh sun cuts them asunder.

And for the distant mountains, note this marvel: «The colours of the shadows in mountains at a great distance take a most lovely blue, much purer than their illuminated portions.» Thus, when the rock is reddish, the lit parts show their own hue the more they are struck by the light. The air itself becomes the painter of those far-off blues.
textosVistos:
OF TREES AND LIGHTS ON THEM.
The best method of practice in representing country scenes, or I should say landscapes with their trees, is to choose them so that the sun is covered with clouds so that the landscape receives an universal light and not the direct light of the sun, which makes the shadows sharp and too strongly different from the lights.
A place is most luminous when it is most remote from mountains.

OF LANDSCAPES.
The colours of the shadows in mountains at a great distance take a most lovely blue, much purer than their illuminated portions. And from this it follows that when the rock of a mountain is reddish the illuminated portions are violet (?) and the more they are lighted the more they display their proper colour.
respuestas.visible: On the treatment of light for landscapes

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The law of proportion in the growth of the branches
respuestas.pregunta: The law of proportion in the growth of the branches
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the order that Nature herself observes in her green children. On that I set down: «The plant which gives out the smallest ramifications will preserve the straightest line in the course of its growth.»

Consider how a tree that divides itself little keeps its shaft true, while one that scatters itself into many boughs bends and swells at every fork. And I noted also: «In starting from the main stem the branches always form a base with a prominence as is shown at a b c d.» That swelling at the junction is no accident — it is the tree's own strength, laid where the limb must bear its weight.
textosVistos: In starting from the main stem the branches always form a base with a prominence as is shown at a b c d.
The plant which gives out the smallest ramifications will preserve the straightest line in the course of its growth.

OF THE SCARS ON TREES.
The scars on trees grow to a greater thickness than is required by the sap of the limb which nourishes them.
respuestas.visible: The law of proportion in the growth of the branches

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The direction of growth
respuestas.pregunta: The direction of growth
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you wish to speak of the growth of plants. On that I have set down careful observations, for nature reveals her order in the smallest twig. Consider the ramification: «The plants which spread very much have the angles of the spaces which divide their branches more obtuse in proportion as their point of origin is lower down; that is nearer to the thickest and oldest portion of the tree. Therefore in the youngest portions of the tree the angles of ramification are more acute.» So it is—the old, heavy limbs open wide, while the young shoots rise sharp and eager.

And mark this: «The lowest branches of those trees which have large leaves and heavy fruits, such as nut-trees, fig-trees and the like, always droop towards the ground.» The weight of leaf and fruit bends them earthward, yet the branch still seeks its light above. Also, «The branches always originate above [in the axis of] the leaves»—each shoot springs from the leaf’s bosom, not below it.

As for the upper shoots of lateral branches, they lie closer to the parent branch than the lower ones, as I have noted. Thus growth is no chaos: every angle, every droop, every origin follows a rule set by the plant’s own nature.
textosVistos:
OF THE RAMIFICATIONS OF PLANTS.
The plants which spread very much have the angles of the spaces which divide their branches more obtuse in proportion as their point of origin is lower down; that is nearer to the thickest and oldest portion of the tree. Therefore in the youngest portions of the tree the angles of ramification are more acute.

The lowest branches of those trees which have large leaves and heavy fruits, such as nut-trees, fig-trees and the like, always droop towards the ground.
The branches always originate above [in the axis of] the leaves.
The upper shoots of the lateral branches of plants lie closer to the parent branch than the lower ones.
respuestas.visible: The direction of growth

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The gradations of shade and colour in leaves
respuestas.pregunta: The gradations of shade and colour in leaves
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you turn your eye to the foliage. A most subtle study, for the leaf is no flat thing but a body caught between light and air. On this I set down: «The shadows of plants are never black, for where the atmosphere penetrates there can never be utter darkness.»

Mark how the eye deceives itself. When a dark leaf stands before the light, «that which is nearest to the eye will be the darkest, and the most distant will be the lightest, not being seen against the atmosphere». And if the light falls from one side, the under side of the leaf shows itself «transparent, with a beautiful green colour verging on yellow» — a hue no shadow could ever give.

So the painter must not reach for black to shade his greenery. Let the air itself do the work, and let the leaf turn lustrous where it catches the ray, for in many cases the under side is transparent and the right side shines.
textosVistos:
OF DARK LEAVES IN FRONT OF TRANSPARENT ONES.
When the leaves are interposed between the light and the eye, then that which is nearest to the eye will be the darkest, and the most distant will be the lightest, not being seen against the atmosphere; and this is seen in the leaves which are away from the centre of the tree, that is towards the light.
The shadows of plants are never black, for where the atmosphere penetrates there can never be utter darkness.

If the light comes from m and the eye is at n the eye will see the colour of the leaves a b all affected by the colour of m —that is of the atmosphere; and b c will be seen from the under side as transparent, with a beautiful green colour verging on yellow.
If m is the luminous body lighting up the leaf s all the eyes that see the under side of this leaf will see it of a beautiful light green, being transparent.
In very many cases the positions of the leaves will be without shadow [or in full light], and their under side will be transparent and the right side lustrous [reflecting light].
respuestas.visible: The gradations of shade and colour in leaves

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The proportions of light and shade in trees
respuestas.pregunta: The proportions of light and shade in trees
respuestas.respuesta: On that I set down: «The trees and plants which are most thickly branched with slender branches ought to have less dark shadow than those trees and plants which, having broader leaves, will cast more shadow.» The painter must weigh the nature of each leaf, for the shadow follows the breadth of the foliage, not the number of twigs.
textosVistos:
OF TREES THAT ARE LIGHTED BY THE SUN AND BY THE ATMOSPHERE.
In trees that are illuminated [both] by the sun and the atmosphere and that have leaves of a dark colour, one side will be illuminated by the atmosphere [only] and in consequence of this light will tend to blueness, while on the other side they will be illuminated by the atmosphere and the sun; and the side which the eye sees illuminated by the sun will reflect light.

OF DEPICTING A FOREST SCENE.
The trees and plants which are most thickly branched with slender branches ought to have less dark shadow than those trees and plants which, having broader leaves, will cast more shadow.

The trees of the landscape stand out but little from each other; because their illuminated portions come against the illuminated portions of those beyond and differ little from them in light and shade.
respuestas.visible: The proportions of light and shade in trees

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The effects of morning light
respuestas.pregunta: The effects of morning light
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the dawn's first embrace upon the world. A subject most dear to my studies of light and shadow. On the trees to the East, when the sun rises, I set down: «When the sun is in the East the trees are darker towards the middle while their edges are light.»

Observe how the great mass of foliage holds its shadow, while the circumference, kissed by the rays, becomes luminous. And for those trees standing to the South and North, the balance is more even, for they receive «almost as much light as shadow», though this proportion shifts as they lean towards the West or the East.

The meadows, too, sing a different song in that hour. I noted that «the verdure of the meadows and of other small plants is of a most beautiful green from being transparent to the sun», a brilliance not found in those fields that turn their backs to the morning. It is a subtle harmony, where the eye's position above or below also alters the seen shadows, for the low eye perceives a greater depth of shade than the high one.
textosVistos:
OF TREES TO THE EAST.
When the sun is in the East the trees are darker towards the middle while their edges are light.

OF TREES TO THE SOUTH.
When the sun is in the east the trees to the South and to the North have almost as much light as shadow. But a greater share of light in proportion as they lie to the West and a greater share of shadow in proportion as they lie to the East.
OF MEADOWS.
If the sun is in the East the verdure of the meadows and of other small plants is of a most beautiful green from being transparent to the sun; this does not occur in the meadows to the West, and in those to the South and North the grass is of a moderately brilliant green.

OF TREES IN THE EAST.
When the sun is in the East the trees seen towards the East will have the light which surrounds them all round their shadows, excepting on the side towards the earth; unless the tree has been pruned [below] in the past year. And the trees to the South and North will be half in shade and half in light, and more or less in shade or in light in proportion as they are more or less to the East or to the West.
The [position of] the eye above or below varies the shadows and lights in trees, inasmuch as the eye placed above sees the tree with the little shadow, and the eye placed below with a great deal of shadow.
The colour of the green in plants varies as much as their species.
respuestas.visible: The effects of morning light

respuestas.id: mapa:en:On the treatment of light for views of towns
respuestas.pregunta: On the treatment of light for views of towns
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the town and its light. On that I set down much, for the painter who would capture a city must first understand the sun's geometry. «When the sun is in the East and the eye is above the centre of a town, the eye will see the Southern part of the town with its roofs half in shade and half in light, and the same towards the North; the Eastern side will be all in shadow and the Western will be all in light.»

Consider then the smoke and the dust, for they obey the same law. «Smoke is seen better and more distinctly on the Eastern side than on the Western when the sun is in the East; and this arises from two causes; the first is that the sun, with its rays, shines through the particles of the smoke and lights them up and makes them visible. The second is that the roofs of the houses seen in the East at this time are in shadow, because their obliquity does not allow of their being illuminated by the sun.»

And mark the difference between the two vapours: «If the sun is in the East the smoke of cities will not be visible in the West, because on that side it is not seen penetrated by the solar rays, nor on a dark background; since the roofs of the houses turn the same side to the eye as they turn towards the sun, and on this light background the smoke is not very visible. But dust, under the same aspect, will look darker than smoke being of denser material than smoke which is moist.»

Thus the eye, placed above the town, reads the hour and the substance of the air from the roofs alone.
textosVistos:
OF LIGHT AND SHADOW IN A TOWN.
When the sun is in the East and the eye is above the centre of a town, the eye will see the Southern part of the town with its roofs half in shade and half in light, and the same towards the North; the Eastern side will be all in shadow and the Western will be all in light.

OF THE SMOKE OF A TOWN.
Smoke is seen better and more distinctly on the Eastern side than on the Western when the sun is in the East; and this arises from two causes; the first is that the sun, with its rays, shines through the particles of the smoke and lights them up and makes them visible. The second is that the roofs of the houses seen in the East at this time are in shadow, because their obliquity does not allow of their being illuminated by the sun. And the same thing occurs with dust; and both one and the other look the lighter in proportion as they are denser, and they are densest towards the middle.

OF SMOKE AND DUST.
If the sun is in the East the smoke of cities will not be visible in the West, because on that side it is not seen penetrated by the solar rays, nor on a dark background; since the roofs of the houses turn the same side to the eye as they turn towards the sun, and on this light background the smoke is not very visible.
But dust, under the same aspect, will look darker than smoke being of denser material than smoke which is moist.
respuestas.visible: On the treatment of light for views of towns

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The forms of trees
respuestas.pregunta: The forms of trees
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, the forms of trees—a subject I hold most dear, for in them one sees the very geometry of nature. On the cherry-tree I set down: «The cherry-tree is of the character of the fir tree as regards its ramification placed in stages round its main stem; and its branches spring, 4 or five or 6 [together] opposite each other; and the tips of the topmost shoots form a pyramid from the middle upwards; and the walnut and oak form a hemisphere from the middle upwards.»

Observe how each species keeps its own rule—the one rising in a spire, the other rounding like a vault of heaven. And note the influence of the sun upon their growth, for I wrote: «In general almost all the upright portions of trees curve somewhat turning the convexity towards the South; and their branches are longer and thicker and more abundant towards the South than towards the North. And this occurs because the sun draws the sap towards that surface of the tree which is nearest to it.» Thus does the painter, who would render a tree truly, study not only its boughs but the light that shapes them.
textosVistos: The bough of the walnut which is only hit and beaten when it has brought to perfection…

The cherry-tree is of the character of the fir tree as regards its ramification placed in stages round its main stem; and its branches spring, 4 or five or 6 [together] opposite each other; and the tips of the topmost shoots form a pyramid from the middle upwards; and the walnut and oak form a hemisphere from the middle upwards.

In general almost all the upright portions of trees curve somewhat turning the convexity towards the South; and their branches are longer and thicker and more abundant towards the South than towards the North. And this occurs because the sun draws the sap towards that surface of the tree which is nearest to it.
And this may be observed if the sun is not screened off by other plants.
respuestas.visible: The forms of trees

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The proportions of light and shade in a leaf
respuestas.pregunta: The proportions of light and shade in a leaf
respuestas.respuesta:
On that I set down: «Sometimes a leaf has three accidents [of light] that is: shade, lustre [reflected light] and transparency [transmitted light]. Thus, if the light were at n as regards the leaf s, and the eye at m, it would see a in full light, b in shadow and c transparent.»

The eye and the light must both be considered, for their positions change what the leaf shows you. «And its shadows are in the same positions as those were of the opposite side.» So, painter, when you work a tree close at hand, remember that if the eye is almost under it, you will see leaves on the upper and the under side together — and the upper side will appear bluer the more it is foreshortened, and a single leaf may show part of its right side and part of its under side, whence you must render it of two colours.
textosVistos:
OF THE SHADOWS OF A LEAF.
Sometimes a leaf has three accidents [of light] that is: shade, lustre [reflected light] and transparency [transmitted light]. Thus, if the light were at n as regards the leaf s, and the eye at m, it would see a in full light, b in shadow and c transparent.

the eye and the light which falls upon it from the opposite side.
And its shadows are in the same positions as those were of the opposite side. Therefore, O Painter! when you do trees close at hand, remember that if the eye is almost under the tree you will see its leaves [some] on the upper and [some] on the under side, and the upper side will be bluer in proportion as they are seen more foreshortened, and the same leaf sometimes shows part of the right side and part of the under side, whence you must make it of two colours.

A leaf with a concave surface seen from the under side and up-side-down will sometimes show itself as half in shade, and half transparent. Thus, if o p is the leaf and the light m and the eye n, this will see o in shadow because the light does not fall upon it between equal angles, neither on the upper nor the under side, and p is lighted on the upper side and the light is transmitted to its under side.
respuestas.visible: The proportions of light and shade in a leaf

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Light and shade on groups of trees
respuestas.pregunta: Light and shade on groups of trees
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of the woodland and its veils of light! On that I set down much, for the eye delights in such subtlety. Consider how trees stand one behind another: «The trees of the landscape stand out but little from each other; because their illuminated portions come against the illuminated portions of those beyond and differ little from them in light and shade.»

Yet in composing them, one must not let them fall into sameness. «In the composition of leafy trees be careful not to repeat too often the same colour of one tree against the same colour of another [behind it]; but vary it with a lighter, or a darker, or a stronger green.» Thus the eye finds its path through the grove.

And when the light comes from behind, see how the nearer boughs turn transparent against the shadow of those beyond: «The topmost part of the first will be in great part transparent and light, and will stand out against the dark portion of the second tree.» So nature herself teaches the painter the play of brightness and gloom.
textosVistos: The trees of the landscape stand out but little from each other; because their illuminated portions come against the illuminated portions of those beyond and differ little from them in light and shade.

In the composition of leafy trees be careful not to repeat too often the same colour of one tree against the same colour of another [behind it]; but vary it with a lighter, or a darker, or a stronger green.

Of trees seen from below and against the light, one beyond the other and near together. The topmost part of the first will be in great part transparent and light, and will stand out against the dark portion of the second tree. And thus it will be with all in succession that are placed under the same conditions.
Let s be the light, and r the eye, c d n the first tree, a b c the second. Then I say that r, the eye, will see the portion c f in great part transparent and lighted by the light s which falls upon it from the opposite side, and it will see it, on a dark ground b c because that is the dark part and shadow of the tree a b c.
But if the eye is placed at t it will see o p dark on the light background n g.
Of the transparent and shadowy parts of trees, that which is nearest to you is the darkest.
respuestas.visible: Light and shade on groups of trees

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The effect of wind on trees
respuestas.pregunta: The effect of wind on trees
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, a question close to my heart! On the bending of trees by the wind I set down: «Trees struck by the force of the wind bend to the side towards which the wind is blowing; and the wind being past they bend in the contrary direction, that is in reverse motion.»

And for the painter who would capture this, remember the dust. «In representing wind, besides the bending of the boughs and the reversing of their leaves towards the quarter whence the wind comes, you should also represent them amid clouds of fine dust mingled with the troubled air.» Observe how the leaves turn their points toward you when the gusts overturn them—a subtle reversal of perspective that reveals the unseen force.
textosVistos: Trees struck by the force of the wind bend to the side towards which the wind is blowing; and the wind being past they bend in the contrary direction, that is in reverse motion.

OF REPRESENTING WIND.
In representing wind, besides the bending of the boughs and the reversing of their leaves towards the quarter whence the wind comes, you should also represent them amid clouds of fine dust mingled with the troubled air.

Describe landscapes with the wind, and the water, and the setting and rising of the sun.
THE WIND.
All the leaves which hung towards the earth by the bending of the shoots with their branches, are turned up side down by the gusts of wind, and here their perspective is reversed; for, if the tree is between you and the quarter of the wind, the leaves which are towards you remain in their natural aspect, while those on the opposite side which ought to have their points in a contrary direction have, by being turned over, their points turned towards you.
respuestas.visible: The effect of wind on trees

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Light and shade on clouds
respuestas.pregunta: Light and shade on clouds
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you turn your eye to the sky. On that I have set down much, for the painter who ignores the heavens neglects the greatest of his models. Observe this: «The shadows in clouds are lighter in proportion as they are nearer to the horizon.» So the base of a cloud, though it be in shade, holds a gentler gloom than its summit, for the air itself and the earth's reflection soften what is below.

Mark also the form of these vapours: «The clouds do not show their rounded forms excepting on the sides which face the sun; on the others the roundness is imperceptible because they are in the shade.» Thus, when the sun stands in the East and the clouds in the West, and you place yourself between them, you shall see the edges of those rounded masses dark, while the portions they surround remain light. For those edges turn toward the upper or lateral sky, which reflects itself upon them.

And take heed of this likeness: «Both the cloud and the tree display no roundness at all on their shaded side.» So the shadow swallows all modelling, and only the side that greets the light reveals the body's turning. If you would paint a cloud truly, paint its light, and let its shade be but a softness without form.
textosVistos: The shadows in clouds are lighter in proportion as they are nearer to the horizon.

OF CLOUDS, SMOKE AND DUST AND THE FLAMES OF A FURNACE OR OF A BURNING KILN.
The clouds do not show their rounded forms excepting on the sides which face the sun; on the others the roundness is imperceptible because they are in the shade.
If the sun is in the East and the clouds in the West, the eye placed between the sun and the clouds sees the edges of the rounded forms composing these clouds as dark, and the portions which are surrounded by this dark [edge] are light. And this occurs because the edges of the rounded forms of these clouds are turned towards the upper or lateral sky, which is reflected in them.
Both the cloud and the tree display no roundness at all on their shaded side.
Describe how the clouds are formed and how they dissolve, and what cause raises vapour.
respuestas.visible: Light and shade on clouds

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The relative thickness of the branches to the trunk
respuestas.pregunta: The relative thickness of the branches to the trunk
respuestas.respuesta:
On that matter I set down a rule that governs both the green and the flowing: «All the branches of a tree at every stage of its height when put together are equal in thickness to the trunk [below them].» And the same holds for water: «All the branches of a water [course] at every stage of its course, if they are of equal rapidity, are equal to the body of the main stream.»

But this holds only when the tree is whole, for I added: «unless the tree is pollard—if so the rule does not hold good.» And note the twist where a minor branch departs: «The branches of trees or plants have a twist wherever a minor branch is given off; and this giving off the branch forms a fork; this said fork occurs between two angles of which the largest will be that which is on the side of the larger branch, and in proportion, unless accident has spoilt it.»

Thus nature balances her limbs against the stem, year by year, as the boughs mature their growth.
textosVistos:
All the branches of a tree at every stage of its height when put together are equal in thickness to the trunk [below them].
All the branches of a water [course] at every stage of its course, if they are of equal rapidity, are equal to the body of the main stream.

If the plant n grows to the thickness shown at m, its branches will correspond [in thickness] to the junction a b in consequence of the growth inside as well as outside.
The branches of trees or plants have a twist wherever a minor branch is given off; and this giving off the branch forms a fork; this said fork occurs between two angles of which the largest will be that which is on the side of the larger branch, and in proportion, unless accident has spoilt it.

Every year when the boughs of a plant [or tree] have made an end of maturing their growth, they will have made, when put together, a thickness equal to that of the main stem; and at every stage of its ramification you will find the thickness of the said main stem; as: i k, g h, e f, c d, a b, will always be equal to each other; unless the tree is pollard—if so the rule does not hold good.
All the branches have a direction which tends to the centre of the tree m.
respuestas.visible: The relative thickness of the branches to the trunk

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Light on branches and leaves
respuestas.pregunta: Light on branches and leaves
respuestas.respuesta:
On that I set down: «Young plants have more transparent leaves and a more lustrous bark than old ones; and particularly the walnut is lighter coloured in May than in September.»

And mark how the sun strikes them: «That part of the body will be most illuminated which is hit by the luminous ray coming between right angles.» So the painter must watch the angle of the light, for it shapes every leaf and twig.
textosVistos: Young plants have more transparent leaves and a more lustrous bark than old ones; and particularly the walnut is lighter coloured in May than in September.
That part of the body will be most illuminated which is hit by the luminous ray coming between right angles.

That part of a tree which has shadow for background, is all of one tone, and wherever the trees or branches are thickest they will be darkest, because there are no little intervals of air. But where the boughs lie against a background of other boughs, the brighter parts are seen lightest and the leaves lustrous from the sunlight falling on them.
respuestas.visible: Light on branches and leaves

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Of the transparency of leaves
respuestas.pregunta: Of the transparency of leaves
respuestas.respuesta:
On the transparency of leaves I set down: «The shadows in transparent leaves seen from the under side are the same shadows as there are on the right side of this leaf, they will show through to the underside together with lights, but the lustre [reflected light] can never show through.»

Yet take care, for I also warned: «Never paint leaves transparent to the sun, because they are confused; and this is because on the transparency of one leaf will be seen the shadow of another leaf which is above it.» Thus the eye may catch the shadow beneath, but never the reflected light — and when the sun strikes at an acute angle, the leaf lets through least of all.
textosVistos: The shadows in transparent leaves seen from the under side are the same shadows as there are on the right side of this leaf, they will show through to the underside together with lights, but the lustre [reflected light] can never show through.

Never paint leaves transparent to the sun, because they are confused; and this is because on the transparency of one leaf will be seen the shadow of another leaf which is above it. This shadow has a distinct outline and a certain depth of shade and sometimes is [as much as] half or a third of the leaf which is shaded; and consequently such an arrangement is very confused and the imitation of it should be avoided.
The light shines least through a leaf when it falls upon it at an acute angle.

OF THE SHADOWS OF A LEAF.
Sometimes a leaf has three accidents [of light] that is: shade, lustre [reflected light] and transparency [transmitted light]. Thus, if the light were at n as regards the leaf s, and the eye at m, it would see a in full light, b in shadow and c transparent.
respuestas.visible: Of the transparency of leaves

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The distribution of light and shade with reference to the position of the spectator
respuestas.pregunta: The distribution of light and shade with reference to the position of the spectator
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of that which governs all my landscapes. The eye's place in the world decides whether a tree stands dark against the sun or bright before it. On that I set down: «The shadows of trees placed in a landscape do not display themselves in the same position in the trees on the right hand and those on the left; still more so if the sun is to the right or left.»

For consider the geometry of it. When the eye sits between the light and the tree, the tree shows itself all lit; when the tree stands between the eye and the light, it is all shadow. But when both eye and tree are placed between darkness and light, then it appears «half in shadow and half in light». So the painter must know where he stands before he sets a single stroke.

And for the trees themselves, I favour the clouded sun. «It is better to do them when the sun is covered with clouds, for then the trees are lighted by the general light of the sky, and the general darkness of the earth.» Thus they show their true form, not the harsh division of direct beams, but the soft modelling that nature herself prefers.
textosVistos:
FROM WHENCE TO DEPICT A LANDSCAPE
Landscapes should be represented so that the trees may be half in light and half in shadow; but it is better to do them when the sun is covered with clouds, for then the trees are lighted by the general light of the sky, and the general darkness of the earth. And then they are darkest in certain parts in proportion as those parts are nearest to the middle of the tree and to the earth.

OF THE HERBS OF THE FIELD.
Of the plants which take a shadow from the plants which spring among them, those which are on this side [in front] of the shadow have the stems lighted up on a background of shadow, and the plants on which the shadows fall have their stems dark on a light background; that is on the background beyond the shadow.
OF TREES WHICH ARE BETWEEN THE EYE AND THE LIGHT.
Of the trees which are between the eye and the light the part in front will be light; but this light will be broken by the ramifications of transparent leaves—being seen from the under side—and lustrous leaves—being seen from the upper side; and the background below and behind will be dark green, being in shadow from the front portion of the said tree. This occurs in trees placed above the eye.

The shadows of trees placed in a landscape do not display themselves in the same position in the trees on the right hand and those on the left; still more so if the sun is to the right or left. As is proved by the 4th which says: Opaque bodies placed between the light and the eye display themselves entirely in shadow; and by the 5th: The eye when placed between the opaque body and the light sees the opaque body entirely illuminated. And by the 6th: When the eye and the opaque body are placed between darkness and light, it will be seen half in shadow and half in light.
respuestas.visible: The distribution of light and shade with reference to the position of the spectator

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The appearance of trees in the distance
respuestas.pregunta: The appearance of trees in the distance
respuestas.respuesta:
On that I set down: «Every object in shadow, of whatever form it may be, at a great distance appears to be spherical.» And so it is with trees—the nearer they stand, the more their true ramification shows; the farther off, the more they lose their parts until the whole is scarce discerned. As I wrote: «The outlines of the ramification of trees, where they lie against the illuminated sky, display a form which more nearly approaches the spherical on proportion as they are remote, and the nearer they are the less they appear in this spherical form.»

The spaces between leaves and branches, too, vanish with distance—they are particles of illuminated air, smaller than the tree, and so are lost to sight sooner than the mass itself. Yet this does not mean they are absent; rather, a confused mixture results, partaking chiefly of the hue which predominates. Thus the eye receives a compounded effect of sky and shadow, blended into one distant tone.
textosVistos:
OF THE SPACES [SHOWING THE SKY] IN TREES THEMSELVES.
The spaces between the parts in the mass of trees, and the spaces between the trees in the air, are, at great distances, invisible to the eye; for, where it is an effort [even] to see the whole it is most difficult to discern the parts.—But a confused mixture is the result, partaking chiefly of the [hue] which predominates. The spaces between the leaves consist of particles of illuminated air which are very much smaller than the tree and are lost sight of sooner than the tree; but it does not therefore follow that they are not there. Hence, necessarily, a compounded [effect] is produced of the sky and of the shadows of the tree in shade, which both together strike the eye which sees them.
OF TREES WHICH CONCEAL THESE SPACES IN ONE ANOTHER.
That part of a tree will show the fewest spaces, behind which a large number of trees are standing between the tree and the air [sky]; thus in the tree a the spaces are not concealed nor in b, as there is no tree behind. But in c only half shows the spaces filled up by the tree d, and part of the tree d is filled up by the tree e and a little farther on all the spaces in the mass of the trees are lost, and only that at the side remains.

OF TREES.
What outlines are seen in trees at a distance against the sky which serves as their background?
The outlines of the ramification of trees, where they lie against the illuminated sky, display a form which more nearly approaches the spherical on proportion as they are remote, and the nearer they are the less they appear in this spherical form; as in the first tree a which, being near to the eye, displays the true form of its ramification; but this shows less in b and is altogether lost in c, where not merely the branches of the tree cannot be seen but the whole tree is distinguished with difficulty. Every object in shadow, of whatever form it may be, at a great distance appears to be spherical. And this occurs because, if it is a square body, at a very short distance it loses its angles, and a little farther off it loses still more of its smaller sides which remain. And thus before the whole is lost [to sight] the parts are lost, being smaller than the whole; as a man, who in such a distant position loses his legs, arms and head before [the mass of] his body, then the outlines of length are lost before those of breadth, and where they have become equal it would be a square if the angles remained; but as they are lost it is round.

All trees seen against the sun are dark towards the middle and this shadow will be of the shape of the tree when apart from others.
The shadows cast by trees on which the sun shines are as dark as those of the middle of the tree.
The shadow cast by a tree is never less than the mass of the tree but becomes taller in proportion as the spot on which it falls, slopes towards the centre of the world.
The shadow will be densest in the middle of the tree when the tree has the fewest branches.
Every branch participates of the central shadow of every other branch and consequently [of that] of the whole tree.
The form of any shadow from a branch or tree is circumscribed by the light which falls from the side whence the light comes; and this illumination gives the shape of the shadow, and this may be of the distance of a mile from the side where the sun is.
If it happens that a cloud should anywhere overshadow some part of a hill the [shadow of the] trees there will change less than in the plains; for these trees on the hills have their branches thicker, because they grow less high each year than in the plains. Therefore as these branches are dark by nature and being so full of shade, the shadow of the clouds cannot darken them any more; but the open spaces between the trees, which have no strong shadow change very much in tone and particularly those which vary from green; that is ploughed lands or fallen mountains or barren lands or rocks. Where the trees are against the atmosphere they appear all the same colour—if indeed they are not very close together or very thickly covered with leaves like the fir and similar trees. When you see the trees from the side from which the sun lights them, you will see them almost all of the same tone, and the shadows in them will be hidden by the leaves in the light, which come between your eye and those shadows.
TREES AT A SHORT DISTANCE.
When the trees are situated between the sun and the eye, beyond the shadow which spreads from their centre, the green of their leaves will be seen transparent; but this transparency will be broken in many places by the leaves and boughs in shadow which will come between you and them, or, in their upper portions, they will be accompanied by many lights reflected from the leaves.
respuestas.visible: The appearance of trees in the distance

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The cast shadow of trees
respuestas.pregunta: The cast shadow of trees
respuestas.respuesta:
On that I set down: «The image of the shadow of any object of uniform breadth can never be [exactly] the same as that of the body which casts it.» So it is with trees—their shadows are not mere copies, for the light bends and the ground slopes, altering the form.

And further: «All trees seen against the sun are dark towards the middle and this shadow will be of the shape of the tree when apart from others.» The shadow cast by a tree is never less than its mass, but grows taller as the ground falls toward the centre of the world. Where branches are fewest, there the shadow is densest, for «every branch participates of the central shadow of every other branch.»

If a cloud veils a hill, the shadows of trees there change less than in the plains—such is the subtlety of light’s play.
textosVistos: The image of the shadow of any object of uniform breadth can never be [exactly] the same as that of the body which casts it.

All trees seen against the sun are dark towards the middle and this shadow will be of the shape of the tree when apart from others.
The shadows cast by trees on which the sun shines are as dark as those of the middle of the tree.
The shadow cast by a tree is never less than the mass of the tree but becomes taller in proportion as the spot on which it falls, slopes towards the centre of the world.
The shadow will be densest in the middle of the tree when the tree has the fewest branches.
Every branch participates of the central shadow of every other branch and consequently [of that] of the whole tree.
The form of any shadow from a branch or tree is circumscribed by the light which falls from the side whence the light comes; and this illumination gives the shape of the shadow, and this may be of the distance of a mile from the side where the sun is.
If it happens that a cloud should anywhere overshadow some part of a hill the [shadow of the] trees there will change less than in the plains; for these trees on the hills have their branches thicker, because they grow less high each year than in the plains. Therefore as these branches are dark by nature and being so full of shade, the shadow of the clouds cannot darken them any more; but the open spaces between the trees, which have no strong shadow change very much in tone and particularly those which vary from green; that is ploughed lands or fallen mountains or barren lands or rocks. Where the trees are against the atmosphere they appear all the same colour—if indeed they are not very close together or very thickly covered with leaves like the fir and similar trees. When you see the trees from the side from which the sun lights them, you will see them almost all of the same tone, and the shadows in them will be hidden by the leaves in the light, which come between your eye and those shadows.
TREES AT A SHORT DISTANCE.
When the trees are situated between the sun and the eye, beyond the shadow which spreads from their centre, the green of their leaves will be seen transparent; but this transparency will be broken in many places by the leaves and boughs in shadow which will come between you and them, or, in their upper portions, they will be accompanied by many lights reflected from the leaves.

OF DEPICTING A FOREST SCENE.
The trees and plants which are most thickly branched with slender branches ought to have less dark shadow than those trees and plants which, having broader leaves, will cast more shadow.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Of rainbows and rain
respuestas.pregunta: Of rainbows and rain
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, the rainbow—a marvel that has long held my pen. On it I set down: «The bow in itself is not in the rain nor in the eye that sees it; though it is generated by the rain, the sun, and the eye.» Thus it is no thing of substance, but a child of three parents meeting in the air.

And mark the position of the observer, for «The rainbow is always seen by the eye that is between the rain and the body of the sun; hence if the sun is in the East and the rain is in the West it will appear on the rain in the West.» So the eye stands as the third partner in this spectacle, and without it the bow would vanish as a dream.
textosVistos:
The colours in the middle of the rainbow mingle together.
The bow in itself is not in the rain nor in the eye that sees it; though it is generated by the rain, the sun, and the eye. The rainbow is always seen by the eye that is between the rain and the body of the sun; hence if the sun is in the East and the rain is in the West it will appear on the rain in the West.

When the air is condensed into rain it would produce a vacuum if the rest of the air did not prevent this by filling its place, as it does with a violent rush; and this is the wind which rises in the summer time, accompanied by heavy rain.
Describe a wind on land and at sea. Describe a storm of rain.
respuestas.visible: Of rainbows and rain

respuestas.id: mapa:en:OF Classification of trees
respuestas.pregunta: OF Classification of trees
respuestas.respuesta: On the classification of trees I set down: «Small, lofty, straggling, thick, that is as to foliage, dark, light, russet, branched at the top; some directed towards the eye, some downwards; with white stems; this transparent in the air, that not; some standing close together, some scattered.»
textosVistos:
TREES.
Small, lofty, straggling, thick, that is as to foliage, dark, light, russet, branched at the top; some directed towards the eye, some downwards; with white stems; this transparent in the air, that not; some standing close together, some scattered.

The trees in a landscape are of various kinds of green, inasmuch as some verge towards blackness, as firs, pines, cypresses, laurels, box and the like. Some tend to yellow such as walnuts, and pears, vines and verdure. Some are both yellowish and dark as chesnuts, holm-oak. Some turn red in autumn as the service-tree, pomegranate, vine, and cherry; and some are whitish as the willow, olive, reeds and the like. Trees are of various forms …

OF THE SPACES [SHOWING THE SKY] IN TREES THEMSELVES.
The spaces between the parts in the mass of trees, and the spaces between the trees in the air, are, at great distances, invisible to the eye; for, where it is an effort [even] to see the whole it is most difficult to discern the parts.—But a confused mixture is the result, partaking chiefly of the [hue] which predominates. The spaces between the leaves consist of particles of illuminated air which are very much smaller than the tree and are lost sight of sooner than the tree; but it does not therefore follow that they are not there. Hence, necessarily, a compounded [effect] is produced of the sky and of the shadows of the tree in shade, which both together strike the eye which sees them.
OF TREES WHICH CONCEAL THESE SPACES IN ONE ANOTHER.
That part of a tree will show the fewest spaces, behind which a large number of trees are standing between the tree and the air [sky]; thus in the tree a the spaces are not concealed nor in b, as there is no tree behind. But in c only half shows the spaces filled up by the tree d, and part of the tree d is filled up by the tree e and a little farther on all the spaces in the mass of the trees are lost, and only that at the side remains.
respuestas.visible: Classification of trees

respuestas.id: mapa:en:A classification of trees according to their colours
respuestas.pregunta: A classification of trees according to their colours
respuestas.respuesta:
On that I set down: «The trees in a landscape are of various kinds of green, inasmuch as some verge towards blackness, as firs, pines, cypresses, laurels, box and the like. Some tend to yellow such as walnuts, and pears, vines and verdure. Some are both yellowish and dark as chesnuts, holm-oak. Some turn red in autumn as the service-tree, pomegranate, vine, and cherry; and some are whitish as the willow, olive, reeds and the like.»

Thus the eye reads the wood not as one mass, but as a harmony of differing greens — dark, yellow, russet, red, and pale — each tree declaring its kind by hue before by form. And in the crowding of the grove, remember this: «The trees of the landscape stand out but little from each other; because their illuminated portions come against the illuminated portions of those beyond and differ little from them in light and shade.» So colour alone must separate what light and shade will not.
textosVistos: The trees in a landscape are of various kinds of green, inasmuch as some verge towards blackness, as firs, pines, cypresses, laurels, box and the like. Some tend to yellow such as walnuts, and pears, vines and verdure. Some are both yellowish and dark as chesnuts, holm-oak. Some turn red in autumn as the service-tree, pomegranate, vine, and cherry; and some are whitish as the willow, olive, reeds and the like. Trees are of various forms …

TREES.
Small, lofty, straggling, thick, that is as to foliage, dark, light, russet, branched at the top; some directed towards the eye, some downwards; with white stems; this transparent in the air, that not; some standing close together, some scattered.

The trees of the landscape stand out but little from each other; because their illuminated portions come against the illuminated portions of those beyond and differ little from them in light and shade.

respuestas.id: mapa:en:The effects of midday light
respuestas.pregunta: The effects of midday light
respuestas.respuesta:
On light at the middle of the day, I set down: «Objects in high light show but little, but between light and shadow they stand out well.» Thus the painter who seeks relief should not place his figures wholly in the glare, for then the eye finds little to grasp; rather let him set them where the brightness falls away into shade, and there the form reveals itself.

For the landscape at that hour, I advised: «To represent a landscape choose that the sun shall be at noon and look towards the West or East and then draw.» And note the trees—«All the trees which are towards the sun and have the atmosphere for their background are dark, and the other trees which lie against that darkness will be black [very dark] in the middle and lighter towards the edges.» So the midday sun gives you strong darks against the air, and the middle of the tree sinks into shadow while its edges catch the light.
textosVistos:
OBJECTS IN HIGH LIGHT SHOW BUT LITTLE, BUT BETWEEN LIGHT AND SHADOW THEY STAND OUT WELL.
To represent a landscape choose that the sun shall be at noon and look towards the West or East and then draw. And if you turn towards the North, every object placed on that side will have no shadow, particularly those which are nearest to the [direction of the] shadow of your head. And if you turn towards the South every object on that side will be wholly in shadow. All the trees which are towards the sun and have the atmosphere for their background are dark, and the other trees which lie against that darkness will be black [very dark] in the middle and lighter towards the edges.

OF TREES TO THE EAST.
When the sun is in the East the trees are darker towards the middle while their edges are light.

OF TREES TO THE SOUTH.
When the sun is in the east the trees to the South and to the North have almost as much light as shadow. But a greater share of light in proportion as they lie to the West and a greater share of shadow in proportion as they lie to the East.
OF MEADOWS.
If the sun is in the East the verdure of the meadows and of other small plants is of a most beautiful green from being transparent to the sun; this does not occur in the meadows to the West, and in those to the South and North the grass is of a moderately brilliant green.
respuestas.visible: The effects of midday light

respuestas.id: mapa:en:On images reflected in water
respuestas.pregunta: On images reflected in water
respuestas.respuesta: Ah, you touch upon a delightful snare for the painter! Many deceive themselves, believing the water simply mirrors what the eye beholds. But I set down: «the water reflects the object from one side and the man sees it from the other». Thus one may see a thing from below, and the water shows it reversed, «from hind part before and upside down». The eye and the water are two witnesses, and they rarely agree.
textosVistos: Painters often deceive themselves, by representing water in which they make the water reflect the objects seen by the man. But the water reflects the object from one side and the man sees it from the other; and it often happens that the painter sees an object from below, and thus one and the same object is seen from hind part before and upside down, because the water shows the image of the object in one way, and the eye sees it in another.

People were to be seen eagerly embarking victuals on various kinds of hastily made barks. But little of the waves were visible in those places where the dark clouds and rain were reflected.
But where the flashes caused by the bolts of heaven were reflected, there were seen as many bright spots, caused by the image of the flashes, as there were waves to reflect them to the eye of the spectator.
The number of the images produced by the flash of lightning on the waves of the water were multiplied in proportion to the distance of the spectator's eye.
So also the number of the images was diminished in proportion as they were nearer the eye which saw them , as it has been proved in the definition of the luminosity of the moon, and of our marine horizon when the sun's rays are reflected in it and the eye which receives the reflection is remote from the sea.

The waves in water magnify the image of an object reflected in it.
Let a be the sun, and n m the ruffled water, b the image of the sun when the water is smooth. Let f be the eye which sees the image in all the waves included within the base of the triangle c e f. Now the sun reflected in the unruffled surface occupied the space c d, while in the ruffled surface it covers all the watery space c e (as is proved in the 4th of my "Perspective") and it will cover more of the water in proportion as the reflected image is remote from the eye [10].
The image of the sun will be more brightly shown in small waves than in large ones—and this is because the reflections or images of the sun are more numerous in the small waves than in large ones, and the more numerous reflections of its radiance give a larger light than the fewer.
Waves which intersect like the scales of a fir cone reflect the image of the sun with the greatest splendour; and this is the case because the images are as many as the ridges of the waves on which the sun shines, and the shadows between these waves are small and not very dark; and the radiance of so many reflections together becomes united in the image which is transmitted to the eye, so that these shadows are imperceptible.
That reflection of the sun will cover most space on the surface of the water which is most remote from the eye which sees it.
Let a be the sun, p q the reflection of the sun; a b is the surface of the water, in which the sun is mirrored, and r the eye which sees this reflection on the surface of the water occupying the space o m. c is the eye at a greater distance from the surface of the water and also from the reflection; hence this reflection covers a larger space of water, by the distance between n and o.
respuestas.visible: On images reflected in water

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Of flower seeds
respuestas.pregunta: Of flower seeds
respuestas.respuesta:
On flower seeds I set down: «All the flowers which turn towards the sun perfect their seeds; but not the others; that is to say those which get only the reflection of the sun.»

Thus the sun is the true master of generation. Those blooms that fix their gaze upon it ripen their offspring; those that dwell in shadow or receive but a borrowed light remain barren. It is a lesson nature writes plainly for any who will observe her.
textosVistos: All the flowers which turn towards the sun perfect their seeds; but not the others; that is to say those which get only the reflection of the sun.

*(Of Grain and other Seeds.)*
Men will fling out of their houses those victuals which were intended to sustain their life.
*(Of Trees, which nourish grafted shoots.)*
Fathers and mothers will be seen to take much more delight in their step-children then in their own children.
*(Of the Censer.)*
Some will go about in white garments with arrogant gestures threatening others with metal and fire which will do no harm at all to them.

Flax is dedicated to death, and to the corruption of mortals. To death, by being used for snares and nets for birds, animals and fish; to corruption, by the flaxen sheets in which the dead are wrapped when they are buried, and who become corrupt in these winding sheets.— And again, this flax does not separate its fibre till it has begun to steep and putrefy, and this is the flower with which garlands and decorations for funerals should be made.
respuestas.visible: Of flower seeds

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Doubts about the deluge
respuestas.pregunta: Doubts about the deluge
respuestas.respuesta:
A doubt indeed, and one I have turned over often. On the universality of that flood, I set down: «Here a doubt arises, and that is: whether the deluge, which happened at the time of Noah, was universal or not. And it would seem not, for the reasons now to be given.» For if the waters were universal upon our spherical globe, they could not move, since water does not move unless it falls—and so the miracle must be called in to explain their going.

On the shells found far from the sea, I answered thus: «If you were to say that the shells which are to be seen within the confines of Italy now, in our days, far from the sea and at such heights, had been brought there by the deluge which left them there, I should answer that if you believe that this deluge rose 7 cubits above the highest mountains—as he who measured it has written—these shells, which always live near the sea-shore, should have been left on the mountains.» And they lie not in a scattered muddle, but «in regular steps and layers—as we see them now in our time.» That is no work of a single passing flood, but of the sea itself, laying down its own record in the clay.
textosVistos:
A DOUBTFUL POINT.
Here a doubt arises, and that is: whether the deluge, which happened at the time of Noah, was universal or not. And it would seem not, for the reasons now to be given: We have it in the Bible that this deluge lasted 40 days and 40 nights of incessant and universal rain, and that this rain rose to ten cubits above the highest mountains in the world. And if it had been that the rain was universal, it would have covered our globe which is spherical in form. And this spherical surface is equally distant in every part, from the centre of its sphere; hence the sphere of the waters being under the same conditions, it is impossible that the water upon it should move, because water, in itself, does not move unless it falls; therefore how could the waters of such a deluge depart, if it is proved that it has no motion? and if it departed how could it move unless it went upwards? Here, then, natural reasons are wanting; hence to remove this doubt it is necessary to call in a miracle to aid us, or else to say that all this water was evaporated by the heat of the sun.
That marine shells could not go up the mountains.

OF THE DELUGE AND OF MARINE SHELLS. If you were to say that the shells which are to be seen within the confines of Italy now, in our days, far from the sea and at such heights, had been brought there by the deluge which left them there, I should answer that if you believe that this deluge rose 7 cubits above the highest mountains— as he who measured it has written—these shells, which always live near the sea-shore, should have been left on the mountains; and not such a little way from the foot of the mountains; nor all at one level, nor in layers upon layers. And if you were to say that these shells are desirous of remaining near to the margin of the sea, and that, as it rose in height, the shells quitted their first home, and followed the increase of the waters up to their highest level; to this I answer, that the cockle is an animal of not more rapid movement than the snail is out of water, or even somewhat slower; because it does not swim, on the contrary it makes a furrow in the sand by means of its sides, and in this furrow it will travel each day from 3 to 4 braccia; therefore this creature, with so slow a motion, could not have travelled from the Adriatic sea as far as Monferrato in Lombardy , which is 250 miles distance, in 40 days; which he has said who took account of the time. And if you say that the waves carried them there, by their gravity they could not move, excepting at the bottom. And if you will not grant me this, confess at least that they would have to stay at the summits of the highest mountains, in the lakes which are enclosed among the mountains, like the lakes of Lario, or of Como and il Maggiore and of Fiesole, and of Perugia, and others.

of the sea was raised, depositing these shells in layers, as may be seen in the cutting at Colle Gonzoli, laid open by the Arno which is wearing away the base of it; in which cutting the said layers of shells are very plainly to be seen in clay of a bluish colour, and various marine objects are found there. And if the earth of our hemisphere is indeed raised by so much higher than it used to be, it must have become by so much lighter by the waters which it lost through the rift between Gibraltar and Ceuta; and all the more the higher it rose, because the weight of the waters which were thus lost would be added to the earth in the other hemisphere. And if the shells had been carried by the muddy deluge they would have been mixed up, and separated from each other amidst the mud, and not in regular steps and layers— as we see them now in our time. The marine shells were not produced away from the sea.
respuestas.visible: Doubts about the deluge

respuestas.id: mapa:en:Book 15 of matters worn away by water
respuestas.pregunta: Book 15 of matters worn away by water
respuestas.respuesta:
Ah, you speak of my fifteenth book. I set down its order at the very head: «Place at the beginning what a river can effect.» For the river is the great agent of change upon the land—it carves, it carries, it consumes.

And I planned its division with care: «First you shall make a book treating of places occupied by fresh waters, and the second by salt waters, and the third, how by the disappearance of these, our parts of the world were made lighter and in consequence more remote from the centre of the world.» Thus the waters, in their presence and their absence, shape the very globe.

Beyond this, I listed the works a river's force may serve—driving back armies by a released flood, bringing down timber from the mountains, raising bridges by the swelling of the waters, and guarding towns against the river's impetus. All these I meant to gather, for in the movement of water lies both ruin and remedy.
textosVistos:
THE ORDER OF THE BOOK.
